common_name: Columbia Giant Blackberry (Extra-Large-Fruited Pacific Northwest Trailing Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing widely and installing a sturdy multi-wire trellis for the long, sprawling canes.

directions: Columbia Giant is a Washington State University release prized for producing some of the largest berries of any trailing blackberry, with thorny, vigorous canes that need a stout multi-wire trellis to support the heavy crop. It is best suited to the cooler, longer-summer conditions of the Pacific Northwest rather than the hot, humid Gulf South, where trailing types of this parentage are more prone to sunscald and disease pressure. Prune out spent floricanes immediately after harvest and train new primocanes along the wires for next year's crop. Full sun and consistent irrigation through fruit swell produce the best berry size.
sources: Washington State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide
Oregon State University Extension — Trailing Blackberry Cultivars

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring in well-drained soil and train onto a trellis; Siskiyou ripens earlier than most other Oregon trailing blackberry releases.

directions: Siskiyou is an Oregon State University trailing blackberry selected for its early ripening window and large, firm, well-flavored fruit on thorny canes. Like most Pacific Northwest trailing blackberries, it performs best where summers are warm but not extremely humid, and it is a lower priority for Gulf Coast gardens than erect, thornless, heat- and disease-tolerant University of Arkansas releases such as Natchez or Ouachita. Train the long canes onto a two- or three-wire trellis, cut fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest, and tie in new primocanes for the following year's crop.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Cultivar Trials
Washington State University Extension — Small Fruit Production

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Appalachian is an erect, thorny type that is self-supporting but benefits from a simple single-wire trellis in windy sites.

directions: Appalachian is an erect, thorny blackberry valued chiefly for its cold hardiness and reliable early-midseason cropping in cooler mid-Atlantic and upland Southern growing areas rather than for Gulf Coast heat tolerance. Berries are medium to large with good, tangy-sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating and preserves. Because it lacks the double-blossom rosette and heat tolerance improvements bred into later University of Arkansas thornless releases, it is better suited to zone 7 and cooler upland gardens than the Deep Gulf South. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest each summer and thin crowded new canes to the strongest 4-6 per plant to maintain fruit size and airflow.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service small fruit breeding records

common_name: Glen Fyne Raspberry (Spine-Free Scottish Mid-Season Red Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring on a two-wire trellis; Glen Fyne is a floricane-fruiting type that crops on the previous season's canes.

directions: Glen Fyne is a Scottish red raspberry from the James Hutton Institute's Glen series, bred for spine-free canes and good midseason fruit quality for the fresh market. It needs a cool, long summer with winter chill to crop well and is not a candidate for Gulf Coast gardens, where summer heat and insufficient winter chill limit floricane raspberry production generally. Grow on a sturdy trellis in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, removing spent floricanes to the ground immediately after harvest and thinning new primocanes to the strongest canes per linear foot of row. Mulch heavily to conserve soil moisture through summer fruiting.
sources: James Hutton Institute — Raspberry Breeding Programme
Scottish Government Rural and Environment Science and Analytical Services — Soft Fruit Cultivar Trials

common_name: Resolve Raspberry (Root Rot-Resistant Scottish Red Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring in well-drained soil; Resolve was bred for resistance to Phytophthora root rot, a problem in poorly drained raspberry plantings.

directions: Resolve is a modern Scottish red raspberry bred by the James Hutton Institute with a specific focus on resistance to Phytophthora root rot, a soil-borne disease that shortens the productive life of raspberry plantings in heavy or poorly drained soils. Like other floricane red raspberries bred in Scotland, it requires substantial winter chill and a cool summer to crop well, making it unsuitable for Gulf Coast zone 8-10 gardens. Grow on a trellis in well-drained, organically rich soil, and if root rot pressure is a concern, plant on raised beds or ridges regardless of cultivar to further improve drainage. Remove fruited floricanes after harvest and manage new primocane numbers to maintain cane vigor.
sources: James Hutton Institute — Raspberry Breeding Programme

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in fall in cold-winter regions, or in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Cavendish is a June-bearing type that fruits the season after a spring planting.

directions: Cavendish is a June-bearing strawberry released by the Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada research station at Kentville, Nova Scotia, bred for the short, cool growing seasons of Atlantic Canada and the northeastern United States. It produces large, firm, bright-red berries with good flavor on vigorous, winter-hardy plants, and it has become a regional standard for home gardens and pick-your-own operations in zones with real winter chill. Because it requires substantial winter cold to flower and crop normally, it is not a fit for Gulf Coast zone 8-10 gardens, where day-neutral or Florida-bred short-day cultivars perform far better. Renew beds every 3-4 years by rooting daughter plants from runners, and mulch over winter in cold-winter climates to protect the crowns.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Kentville Research and Development Centre strawberry releases
Nova Scotia Department of Agriculture — Strawberry Cultivar Guide

common_name: Elyana Strawberry (Firm Short-Day Strawberry for Winter Production)

planting.note: In zone 9, set out plugs or bare-root plants in fall for winter-into-spring harvest, following the same short-day production schedule used for Camarosa and Chandler.

directions: Elyana is a short-day strawberry cultivar widely grown under protected and open-field winter production systems in Mediterranean climates, prized for firm, glossy, conical fruit with good shelf life and a productive, concentrated harvest window. Its short-day flowering response and winter-production habit are similar to the Florida- and California-bred cultivars already common in Gulf Coast gardens, making it a reasonable candidate for the same fall-planted, winter-harvested system used for Camarosa and Chandler, though it is far less commonly available through US retail nurseries. Plant in raised, well-drained beds in full sun, and provide floating row cover on the occasional hard-freeze night during winter fruiting.
sources: European strawberry variety trial reports (Spain/Mediterranean short-day production)

common_name: Puget Reliance Strawberry (Disease-Resistant Pacific Northwest Processing Strawberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns or plugs in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Puget Reliance is a June-bearing type developed for the cool, wet growing conditions of western Washington.

directions: Puget Reliance is a June-bearing strawberry developed by Washington State University's Puyallup research program for the cool, humid growing conditions of the Pacific Northwest, where it was bred for improved resistance to red stele and Verticillium wilt compared to older regional standards. It produces firm, richly flavored fruit well suited to both fresh eating and processing, but its chilling requirement and adaptation to mild, wet summers make it a poor match for Gulf Coast heat and humidity. Plant in raised beds with excellent drainage, renew plantings every 3-4 years, and remove the first season's flowers on new plantings to build stronger crowns before full production.
sources: Washington State University Puyallup Research and Extension Center — Strawberry Breeding Program
Pacific Northwest Extension — Strawberry Production Guide

common_name: Pax Gooseberry (Nearly Spine-Free Mildew-Resistant Dessert Gooseberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil; Pax is valued for its almost thornless canes, which make pruning and harvest far more pleasant than with traditional spiny gooseberries.

directions: Pax is an English dessert gooseberry bred at East Malling Research Station, selected both for its nearly spine-free canes — a notable improvement in ease of harvest over most traditional gooseberry cultivars — and for good resistance to American gooseberry mildew. The medium-large, dark-red fruit has a sweet, rich flavor good for fresh eating as well as cooking. Like other gooseberries, it prefers cool, moist summers and struggles in Gulf Coast heat and humidity; afternoon shade and heavy mulch help where summers are hot. Prune to an open-centered framework of 8-10 main branches in winter, removing low, crossing, and overly dense growth to maintain airflow and fruit size.
sources: East Malling Research — Gooseberry Breeding Programme
Royal Horticultural Society — Gooseberry Cultivar Guide

common_name: Ben Loyal Black Currant (Early-Season Scottish Black Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall through early spring in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Ben Loyal is part of the Scottish Crop Research Institute's 'Ben' series of black currants, bred at the former Mylnefield research station (now part of the James Hutton Institute) for heavy yields of large, strongly aromatic black fruit used mainly for jams, syrups, and cordials rather than fresh eating. It flowers relatively early for a Ben-series cultivar, so late spring frosts can reduce fruit set in exposed sites. Like all black currants, it needs real winter chill and cool summers to perform well and is not suited to Gulf Coast zone 8-10 conditions, where summer heat and insufficient chill limit black currant cropping generally. Prune out roughly a third of the oldest wood each dormant season to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous young fruiting canes.
sources: James Hutton Institute (formerly Scottish Crop Research Institute) — Black Currant Breeding Programme
Royal Horticultural Society — Currant Cultivar Guide
